title: Fatal police raid sparks questions
article: Why did Toronto Police raid the home of a suspected marijuana dealer in the middle of the night -- especially when they knew there was a passel of children likely asleep in the house?
That's one of the key questions surrounding the sudden death a week ago of Paulo Medeiros at his Mulock Avenue home in the St. Clair Avenue West and Keele Street area.
The 34-year-old Mr. Medeiros, who reportedly weighed more than 300 pounds, died after a struggle with some of the 14 police officers who were involved in the raid early last Friday morning.

In the room as he collapsed, and for the fight and double pepper-spraying which preceded it, was his wife, Lucy, and one of the couple's six children, a son who is between five and seven years old. The little boy, police sources say, was sleeping in his parents' bedroom on a cot when police burst in.
The incident is under investigation by the province's independent Special Investigations Unit, which probes cases where civilians are killed or seriously hurt while in police custody.

The Globe and Mail has learned that police making such raids sometimes secure what are called "night warrants" from judges or justices of the peace, which specifically allow them to make unannounced arrests under cover of darkness, either because it is only in the wee hours that alleged dealers have drug product at hand or for reasons of officer safety.

According to police sources, about a pound of marijuana was seized at the Medeiros house, which sits on a quiet street of modest homes in a mixed residential and industrial part of Toronto's west end.
Yesterday, none of the family was at the house, which has both a religious plate at the front door typical of the working-class Portuguese neighbourhood and high-tech surveillance cameras.
Callers were referred to a relative's home further north on Mulock, but there, family members refused comment.

The police team, composed of officers from 12 Division's major crime squad and a newly formed task force designed to focus on area drug dens and trouble spots and all wearing what are called raid jackets reading police on the front, forced their way into the house about 1:30 a.m.
According to Globe sources, police knew beforehand there were at least five children ranging from toddlers to teenagers who probably would be in the house.

As police tried to enter his bedroom, just off the front hall, sources say Mr. Medeiros jammed the door shut on one officer's hand, cutting him for about six stitches. When officers got through the door, Mr. Medeiros then attempted to flee, and the fight was on.
He was pepper-sprayed once, The Globe has learned, to no effect, and then sprayed a second time, causing him to fall onto the floor on his stomach atop one of the officers.
Though both Mrs. Medeiros and the little boy were in the room, and though the fumes were thick, neither was close enough to have been directly sprayed.
Officers then tried to handcuff Mr. Medeiros and, in the process, he was struck on the legs with a baton.
So furiously was he resisting, police sources say, that officers had to use two sets of handcuffs to subdue him.
At this point, The Globe has learned, the short but burly man was helped to his feet, and sat on the bed, apparently catching his breath.
Moments later, he abruptly collapsed.
An autopsy has revealed no anatomical cause of death, with further test results pending.

The house first came to police attention more than a year ago. Sporadic surveillance resumed last fall and lasted through this month, after citizens in the area allegedly told police of concern for the youngsters living there.
Each time, officers allegedly noted a large number of cars stopping by the house, with drivers briefly entering the premises and returning after only a few minutes.
Sometimes, police sources say, these visits were so short that drivers left the cars running while they went in.

Mr. Medeiros's death, and the raid during which it occurred, serve to illustrate the great divide between the stated intention of the federal government to decriminalize the possession of small amounts of marijuana and the pressures, real or perceived, upon local police forces to enforce laws against drug-dealing.
Under the last government's proposed decriminalization bill, possession of less than 15 grams of marijuana -- or about half an ounce -- would result in a fine comparable to those for traffic tickets.
